### Palovarotene (Sohonos) — NDA 215559

- Therapeutic area: Rare Disease / Genetic / Metabolic-genetic (fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva)
- Sponsor: Ipsen Biopharmaceuticals (originally Clementia Pharmaceuticals)
- Approval year: 2023
- Trial: PVO-1A-301 (MOVE), NCT03312634, single-arm, open-label; external control = natural history study PVO-1A-001 (NCT02322255). Principal FAS: MOVE N=97, NHS N=101.
- Context: prespecified primary analysis (Bayesian compound Poisson with square-root transform) failed (Pr(ratio<1)=0.65). Approval rested on post hoc analyses: Applicant's weighted linear mixed-effects model (wLME) and FDA's GEE landmark, random-slope, and ordinal logistic analyses. FDA [IR p.44]: "The prespecified Bayesian compound Poisson model incorporating square root transformation is not valid and appears to have a bias against palovarotene due to the more frequent assessment in Study 301."

#### Model 1: Annualized new HO volume, longest follow-up (post hoc "alternative analysis of primary interest"; originally the primary analysis in the 10 July 2017 protocol)

- model_family: linear mixed model (random intercept), weighted (wLME)
- Response: annualized new HO = change in total HO volume from baseline at the subject's longest follow-up / follow-up years; no square-root transform; negative values kept [IR Table 13 footnote; SAP §2.4.4 p.38]
- Fixed effects: study/treatment indicator (MOVE vs NHS) + baseline HO volume/age ("the only covariate") [SAP p.38]
- Random effects: subject intercept. SAP verbatim [p.38]: "A subject-level random effect will be used to account for the correlation among repeated measures on the same subject as subjects may contribute follow-up from both the NHS and the current study." Only subjects who moved from NHS to MOVE (n=39) contribute 2 observations.
- Weights: follow-up length. SAP [p.38]: "The LME model will be fitted using only a subject's observations associated with the longest follow-up in the NHS and the current study with weights used to account for the different lengths of observed subject follow-up."
- SAS code (verbatim, SAP p.38): `proc mixed data=data; class treat usubjid; model annrate_newho = treat basetot_bage /s; random usubjid; lsmeans treat/pdiff=control('0') cl; weight fup; run;`
- Covariance: no R-side structure. Variance comes from the random subject intercept plus weighted residual (SAP code has no REPEATED statement).
- Fallback: Not stated
- df method: Not stated (no DDFM option in SAP code)
- Estimation: Not stated (SAS PROC MIXED default would be REML; not explicit)
- Time coding: none (single annualized value per subject per study; assumes constant rate of HO accrual)
- Estimand/contrast: LS-mean difference in annualized new HO volume, MOVE − NHS
- Missing data: SAP [p.38] "Missing at random will be assumed for the primary analysis and no imputation of missing data performed."
- MNAR sensitivity: SAP [p.42] tipping point. Subjects who discontinued have new HO imputed "using the wLME-modeled treatment effect," scaled to 0/25/50/75/100% reduction of the treatment effect (100% = NHS distribution). Results Not stated in IR.
- Other prespecified wLME sensitivities [SAP p.41-42]: additional baseline covariates (HO/age, age, sex, months since last flare-up, CAJIS); propensity-score quartile as a 5-level factor; restriction to 1-year (≤15 mo) and 2-year (≤27 mo) follow-up; five "series" with zeroing out and square-root variants; subgroup analyses by sex, Asian ancestry, age, and age×sex.
- Software: SAS 9.4 or higher [SAP p.38, §4 p.59]
- Result [IR Table 13, p.34]: MOVE N=97 mean annualized new HO 9.4 (SE 3.1) cm3/yr; NHS N=101 23.7 (SE 4.9); LS-mean difference −10.9 (95% CI −21.2, −0.6), nominal p=0.039. Publication [Pub abstract]: "wLME results were similar (54% reduction fitted; nominal p = 0.039)."
- FDA comments [IR p.33-34, p.43]: "estimated treatment effect based on various lengths of follow-up could be difficult to interpret without the assumption of a constant rate of change in HO". FDA ran landmark GEE (Model 5) to test sensitivity to this assumption. Applicant's propensity-score matching/weighting sensitivity analyses [IR Table 22] "did not change the conclusion of the wLME analysis."

#### Model 2: Annualized new HO, NHS→MOVE transition subjects (Applicant within-subject sensitivity)

- model_family: linear mixed model (random intercept), weighted
- Response: annualized new HO; analysis (a) uses the longest follow-up in each study, analysis (b) uses the last 12-month change in NHS vs the first 12-month change in MOVE [IR Table 26, p.47]
- Fixed effects: study (MOVE vs NHS); baseline rate of HO [IR Table 26 footnote: "Analysis covariate: baseline rate of HO; random subject effect."; SAP p.41]
- Random effects: subject intercept
- Covariance/df/estimation: Not stated
- Result [IR Table 26]: N=39 per study. (a) MOVE 8.1 (SE 4.0) vs NHS 16.7 (3.3), difference −8.6 (−17.7, 0.5), p=0.0634. (b) 4.9 (4.9) vs 18.2 (5.2), difference −13.2 (−25.7, −0.8), p=0.0377.
- FDA comment: within-subject comparisons "may potentially have reduced unmeasured confounding."
- Software: SAS 9.4+ [SAP §4]

#### Model 3: Annualized new HO with large values capped (threshold sensitivity; Applicant ISE + FDA)

- model_family: linear mixed model (random intercept)
- Response: annualized new HO with values above a threshold (100, 90, 70, 50, 30 cm3/yr) set to the threshold
- Fixed effects [IR Table 41/42 footnote]: "fixed effects of treatment and baseline total HO/baseline age and a random subject effect"
- Random effects: subject
- Covariance/df/estimation: Not stated
- Result [IR Table 41, p.89]: cap 100: MOVE 8.7 vs NHS 17.7, difference −9.1 (−15.8, −2.3), p=0.01, Wilcoxon p=0.0003. FDA Table 42: cap 30 gives −5.5 (−9.1, −1.8), p=0.004.
- FDA comment: "the difference in the original wLME analysis was not likely driven by extreme large values of subjects in NHS."

#### Model 4: Annualized new HO — prespecified GEE sensitivity (Applicant, SAP v1.3.1)

- model_family: GEE (marginal, not mixed-effects)
- SAP verbatim [p.42]: "A GEE model will be fit to the annualized change in new HO and the empirical variance estimator will be used for inference. Weights will be used to account for the different lengths of observed subject follow-up. Baseline HO volume divided by age will be included in the model as a covariate and a compound-symmetric working correlation matrix will be used."
- Covariance: CS working correlation, empirical (sandwich) SE
- Result: Not stated (IR does not report the Applicant's GEE separately)
- Software: SAS 9.4+ [SAP §4]

#### Model 5: Annualized new HO at Month 12 — FDA landmark analyses (FDA post hoc)

- model_family: GEE (marginal)
- Response: change in HO / follow-up duration over a 12-month window; no square-root transform; negatives kept [IR Table 20 footnote a]
- Fixed effects: treatment + covariate set 1 (baseline HO/age), set 2 (+ sex, baseline age), or set 3 (+ baseline CAJIS, time since last flare-up)
- Covariance: Not stated (working correlation not given). "a robust sandwich variance estimator was used to account for heteroscedasticity in variance" [IR p.43]
- Missing data: three ways of handling subjects without Month-12 data, plus MI with a delta penalty. IR [Table 20 footnote]: "Conclusion from the multiple imputation-based approach will be overturned when a penalty greater than 45 cm3/year is added to the imputed values in treated subjects."
- Result [IR Table 20, p.43]: Month-12 completers (93 vs 90), cov1: 6.7 (2.4) vs 22.0 (6.4), difference −15.3 (−28.5, −2.1), p=0.0229. All subjects (97 vs 101), cov3: −13.9 (−26.3, −1.5), p=0.0275. MI (cov3): −14.4 (−28.1, −0.7), p=0.0395.
- FDA rationale: a landmark analysis "does not rely on assumptions of a constant rate of change."
- Software: Not stated

#### Model 6: Change in HO volume over time — FDA random-slope model (FDA post hoc)

- model_family: random-coefficients/random-slope
- IR verbatim [p.44]: "The FDA review team also conducted analyses based on a random slope model, with change in HO volume from baseline as the response and time from baseline as a continuous variable, adjusting for relevant baseline covariates. Results from these analyses are similar to results of the landmark analyses with generally smaller nominal p-values. We note that the random slope model also assumes a constant rate of change, similar to the Applicant's wLME method, but it is more efficient as it utilizes all available observations rather than just the last observation."
- Fixed effects: treatment, time (continuous), "relevant baseline covariates" (not listed); a treatment×time term is implied but not stated
- Random effects: random slope on time (random intercept Not stated)
- Covariance/df/estimation/software: Not stated
- Result: Not stated numerically ("similar ... with generally smaller nominal p-values")

#### Model 7: New HO (count of regions × volume per region) — Bayesian compound Poisson (prespecified primary; failed)

- model_family: other — Bayesian hierarchical compound Poisson. Poisson count of body regions with new HO uses a subject-level gamma-distributed rate (a random effect giving a negative binomial marginal), combined with a normal model for sqrt(volume) per region. Included because the subject-level gamma rate is a random effect for repeated scans.
- SAP verbatim [§2.4.4 p.35]: "The subject-level rate λ follows a gamma distribution and accounts for potential correlation in measurements from the same subject ... Therefore, the marginal distribution of the number of body regions with new HO follows a negative binomial distribution."
- Fixed effects: treatment on-time indicator (θ1 for rate, θ2 for volume), sex, age (<18 vs ≥18); scan-interval duration w as exposure; region-specific α parameters with left/right constraints
- Time: interval-level (scan j with duration w)
- Software: R v3.5.0 or later [SAP p.38, §4]
- Result [IR Table 11]: with sqrt: median ratio 0.95 (0.74, 1.22), Pr(ratio<1)=0.65. Without sqrt: posterior probability 99.4% [Pub].
- FDA: judged invalid and biased against the drug because of the 6- vs 12-month scan schedule interacting with the sqrt transform [IR p.44]

Notes: flare-up rate used negative binomial regression with log-years offset, and Month-12 body-region counts used NB regression [SAP p.44]. These have no random effects and are not mixed models. Exploratory endpoints (CAJIS, FOP-PFQ, PROMIS) were descriptive only [SAP p.45].

#### Verbatim specification excerpts

##### Model 1: Annualized new HO volume, longest follow-up (post hoc "alternative analysis of primary interest"; originally the primary analysis in the 10 July 2017 protocol)

> "The method for the primary efficacy analysis (a Bayesian analysis of a compound Poisson distribution) described in Protocol Amendment 1 and this SAP is different from the method included in the original protocol dated 10 July 2017 (weighted linear mixed effects model). The method and accompanying power simulations in the original protocol were based on a March 2017 evaluation of the available NHS 12-month WBCT data. In a subsequent dataset, increased variability in the change from baseline in new HO resulted in a substantive power decrease for the weighted linear mixed effects model."
>
> — SAP v1.3.1 §1.9.1, p. 11 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/34/NCT03312634/SAP_003.pdf)

> "Additional supportive analyses including the weighted mixed linear effect (wMLE) analysis with and without the square-root transformation will also be performed. The wLME analysis without the square-root transformation was previously the primary efficacy analysis, before the Bayesian compound Poisson analysis was added in Amendment 1 of the protocol. This wLME analysis without square-root transformation is referred to as the alternative analysis of primary interest. A subject-level random effect will be used to account for the correlation among repeated measures on the same subject as subjects may contribute follow-up from both the NHS and the current study. Baseline HO volume divided by age will be the only covariate included in the model, in addition to the factor identifying study of origin. The LME model will be fitted using only a subject’s observations associated with the longest follow-up in the NHS and the current study with weights used to account for the different lengths of observed subject follow-up. Missing at random will be assumed for the primary analysis and no imputation of missing data performed."
>
> — SAP v1.3.1 §2.4.4, p. 38 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/34/NCT03312634/SAP_003.pdf)

```sas
proc mixed data=data;
                class treat usubjid;
                model annrate_newho = treat basetot_bage /s;
                random usubjid;
                lsmeans treat/pdiff=control('0') cl;
                weight fup;
run;
```

— SAP v1.3.1 §2.4.4, p. 38 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/34/NCT03312634/SAP_003.pdf)

> "In this code, treat is a binary indicator for study (1=MOVE, 0=NHS); usubjid is a unique identifier of subjects (used across all FOP studies); annrate_newho is the annualized rate of new HO; and fup is follow-up in years."
>
> — SAP v1.3.1 §2.4.4, p. 38 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/34/NCT03312634/SAP_003.pdf)

> "Adjustment for additional baseline covariates: This sensitivity analysis will extend the primary efficacy analysis to include additional baseline covariates. These will include baseline HO volume divided by age, age, sex, months since last flare-up, and CAJIS. The palovarotene treatment effect will be estimated using the Bayesian compound Poisson distribution with all covariates included. A similar wLME will also be performed. [...] Propensity score quartile will be used as the only covariate in the Bayesian compound Poisson analysis. wLME will be conducted for each quartile and overall using the 5-level factor as a covariate (in addition to treatment)."
>
> — SAP v1.3.1 §2.4.4 sensitivity analyses, p. 41 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/34/NCT03312634/SAP_003.pdf)

> "Analysis restricting subjects to specific durations of follow-up: The WBCT dataset will be restricted to observations associated up to 1-year – interpreted as assessments within the first 15 months of study participation (i.e., midway between Month 12 and Month 18 for MOVE) – and, separately, with up to 2-years of follow-up – interpreted as assessments within the first 27 months of study participation. The analysis method will be wLME."
>
> — SAP v1.3.1 §2.4.4 sensitivity analyses, p. 42 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/34/NCT03312634/SAP_003.pdf)

> "Missing data sensitivity analysis using a tipping point approach: Subjects who discontinue the MOVE study will have volume of new HO imputed using the wLME-modeled treatment effect. The multiple imputations will be scaled to induce 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% reductions in the palovarotene treatment effect. The 0% corresponds to subjects who discontinue the MOVE Trial having the same distribution for number of body regions with new HO and change in HO volume per region as the MOVE subjects who did not discontinue; and 100% corresponds to subjects who discontinued the MOVE Trial having the same distributions as the NHS subjects. Missing data will be imputed for the visits in MOVE that were either missed or would have been missed due to study discontinuation prior to December 4, 2019 / January 24, 2020. Analyses in which subjects who discontinue the NHS have volume of new HO imputed may also be considered, while noting that the majority of subjects who discontinued NHS did so to enroll in an interventional study, e.g., MOVE or less frequently, Study PVO-1A-201."
>
> — SAP v1.3.1 §2.4.4 sensitivity analyses, p. 42 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/34/NCT03312634/SAP_003.pdf)

> "The Applicant’s post hoc wLME analysis with baseline annualized HO (calculated as baseline total HO volume divided by baseline age) as the only covariate achieved nominal significance (Table 13). In this analysis, the annualized new HO for each subject was calculated using the change in total HO volume from baseline associated with the longest follow-up divided by the length of follow-up. The length of follow-up varied substantially among subjects and between studies. For example, annualized new HO was based on the Month 18 observation for 66% of subjects in Study 301 and the Month 36 observation for 32% of subjects in the NHS. The wLME model accounted for the various follow-up lengths using a weighted approach. We note that the estimated treatment effect based on various lengths of follow-up could be difficult to interpret without the assumption of a constant rate of change in HO."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review § Applicant’s Post Hoc wLME, p. 43 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "wLME analyses: subject level random effect included to account for the correlation among repeated measures on the same subject for those who transitioned from NHS to Study 301; No square root transformation, negative new HO included Covariates: annualized HO at baseline calculated by dividing baseline HO by baseline age; response variable- annualized change in HO at last visit."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review Table 13 footnote, p. 43 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "As noted previously, the Applicant’s post hoc wLME analysis (Table 13), based on the CT scan associated with the longest follow-up and without square root transformation, achieved nominal statistical significance. However, results from the Applicant’s wLME could be difficult to interpret as the annualized new HO for each subject was based on various length of follow-up. To assess whether the conclusion is sensitive to the assumption of a constant rate of change, we compared the changes in HO volume between Study 301 and NHS subjects during a 12-month observation period as a landmark analysis given that the majority of the subjects provided 12-month data, which does not rely on assumptions of a constant rate of change. We performed the landmark analyses using different methods for subjects who did not have 12-month data to investigate the consistency of findings. For all these analyses, a robust sandwich variance estimator was used to account for heteroscedasticity in variance."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review FDA assessment, p. 52 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "To assess the impact of subject differences between Study 301 and the NHS, the Applicant conducted sensitivity analyses by adjusting for additional baseline covariates, including the propensity score quartile, and performing matching and weighting based on propensity score among subjects who did not enroll in both the NHS and Study 301 (i.e., nontransition subjects, Table 22). Results from these analyses did not change the conclusion of the wLME analysis (Table 13)."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review, p. 55 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

##### Model 2: Annualized new HO, NHS→MOVE transition subjects (Applicant within-subject sensitivity)

> "Restriction to subjects contributing follow-up for both the NHS and MOVE Trial: This analysis will use the wLME analysis method on the subset of the MOVE subjects who transitioned from the NHS and have annualized rates of new HO for both studies. Baseline HO volume divided by age will be the only covariate included in the model, in addition to the factor identifying the study of origin."
>
> — SAP v1.3.1 §2.4.4 sensitivity analyses, p. 41 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/34/NCT03312634/SAP_003.pdf)

> "The Applicant performed analyses limited to subjects who transitioned from the NHS to Study 301 (i.e., baseline control). One of the Applicant’s analyses compared the observations associated with the longest follow-up within each study. The other analysis compared the last 12-month change of HO in the NHS with the first 12-month change in Study 301. Results from the two analyses favored palovarotene (Table 26)."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review, p. 57 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "Analysis covariate: baseline rate of HO; random subject effect."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review Table 26 footnote, p. 57 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "These within-subject comparisons complemented a between-subject comparison by using each subject’s own observations in the NHS as the control, which may potentially have reduced unmeasured confounding."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review, p. 57 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

##### Model 3: Annualized new HO with large values capped (threshold sensitivity; Applicant ISE + FDA)

> "To investigate robustness of the weighted linear mixed effects (wLME) results to the impact of extreme large values of annualized new HO, the Applicant performed a threshold analysis with a threshold of 100 cm3/year. In this analysis, the values of annualized new HO greater than 100 cm3/year were replaced with the threshold 100 cm3/year (Table 41). Similar analyses with different thresholds from 90 cm3/year (new HO >90 cm3/year set to 90 cm3/year) to 30 were performed (Table 42). These analyses indicate that the difference in the original wLME analysis was not likely driven by extreme large values of subjects in NHS."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review, p. 97 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "Source: Table 25 in ISE. Results were from a mixed model with dependent variable annualized new HO and independent variables including fixed effects of treatment and baseline total HO/baseline age and a random subject effect."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review Table 41 footnote, p. 98 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

##### Model 4: Annualized new HO — prespecified GEE sensitivity (Applicant, SAP v1.3.1)

> "Analysis using generalized estimating equations (GEE): A GEE model will be fit to the annualized change in new HO and the empirical variance estimator will be used for inference. Weights will be used to account for the different lengths of observed subject follow-up. Baseline HO volume divided by age will be included in the model as a covariate and a compound-symmetric working correlation matrix will be used. The GEE model takes a different approach to account for within-subject correlation compared to the primary analysis."
>
> — SAP v1.3.1 §2.4.4 sensitivity analyses, p. 42 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/34/NCT03312634/SAP_003.pdf)

##### Model 5: Annualized new HO at Month 12 — FDA landmark analyses (FDA post hoc)

> "To assess whether the conclusion is sensitive to the assumption of a constant rate of change, we compared the changes in HO volume between Study 301 and NHS subjects during a 12-month observation period as a landmark analysis given that the majority of the subjects provided 12-month data, which does not rely on assumptions of a constant rate of change. We performed the landmark analyses using different methods for subjects who did not have 12-month data to investigate the consistency of findings. For all these analyses, a robust sandwich variance estimator was used to account for heteroscedasticity in variance."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review FDA assessment, p. 52 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "Generalized estimating equation, no square root transformation, negative new HO included; Endpoint: annualized new HO calculated by dividing change in HO by the follow-up duration [...] Covariates 1: baseline rate of HO: baseline total HO divided by baseline age; covariates 2: baseline rate of HO, sex, baseline age; covariates 3: baseline rate of HO, sex, baseline age, baseline CAJIS, time since last flare-up [...] Conclusion from the multiple imputation-based approach will be overturned when a penalty greater than 45 cm3 /year is added to the imputed values in treated subjects."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review Table 20 footnotes, p. 52 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

##### Model 6: Change in HO volume over time — FDA random-slope model (FDA post hoc)

> "The FDA review team also conducted analyses based on a random slope model, with change in HO volume from baseline as the response and time from baseline as a continuous variable, adjusting for relevant baseline covariates. Results from these analyses are similar to results of the landmark analyses with generally smaller nominal p-values. We note that the random slope model also assumes a constant rate of change, similar to the Applicant’s wLME method, but it is more efficient as it utilizes all available observations rather than just the last observation."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review FDA assessment, p. 53 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

##### Model 7: New HO (count of regions × volume per region) — Bayesian compound Poisson (prespecified primary; failed)

> "The change in new HO volume is modeled using a Bayesian compound Poisson distribution. [...] follows a gamma distribution and accounts for potential correlation in measurements from the same subject; 𝑡(𝑖𝑗) is an indicator function equal to 1 if the subject was on treatment at the time of the 𝑗th WBCT scan and 0 if the subject was not on treatment. Therefore, the marginal distribution of the number of body regions with new HO follows a negative binomial distribution, which requires much less restrictive assumptions than a Poisson distribution and does not tend to result in an underestimate of the variance."
>
> — SAP v1.3.1 §2.4.4, p. 35 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/34/NCT03312634/SAP_003.pdf)

> "The Bayesian compound Poisson model will be fitted using the R statistical computing language and environment. The R programs will be run using v3.5.0 or later; packages used, including version number, will be identified in the CSR."
>
> — SAP v1.3.1 §2.4.4, p. 38 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/34/NCT03312634/SAP_003.pdf)

> "The prespecified primary analysis for the primary endpoint was based on a Bayesian compound Poisson model. The Bayesian compound model was estimated based on the number of regions with positive new HO and the average growth per region where positive new HO occurred since the previous WBCT scan. Negative new HO values were set to 0 in the analyses. The prespecified analysis included a square root transformation of each change in HO since the previous scan by region. The Applicant chose this statistical model “to more appropriately accommodate the high degree of variability in the volume of new HO assessed by WBCT.” The square root transformation was included in the Bayesian compound Poisson analysis because simulations suggested that if palovarotene reduced the probability of new HO as much or more than it reduced the new HO volume given new HO, introducing a square root transformation could marginally increase power. Additionally, square root transformation would likely decrease the variance of the endpoint by shrinking any extremely large values of new HO volume."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review, p. 40 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "The prespecified Bayesian compound Poisson model incorporating square root transformation is not valid and appears to have a bias against palovarotene due to the more frequent assessment in Study 301. FDA finds it reasonable to use valid and more appropriate post hoc analyses to assess evidence of efficacy in this specific setting."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review Conclusion, p. 53 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215559Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

### Cipaglucosidase alfa-atga (Pombiliti) — BLA 761204

- Therapeutic area: Rare Disease / Genetic / Metabolic-genetic (late-onset Pompe disease)
- Sponsor: Amicus Therapeutics
- Approval year: 2023
- Trial: ATB200-03 / PROPEL, NCT03729362. Randomized 2:1, double-blind, active-controlled (alglucosidase alfa + placebo). ITT: cipa-mig N=85, comparator N=38.

#### Model 1: Change from baseline in 6MWD at Week 52 (primary)

- model_family: MMRM
- Response: change from baseline at all post-baseline visits [SAP §8.5.1 p.35]
- Fixed effects (SAP verbatim, p.35): "the fixed, categorical effects of treatment, time (ie, visit), treatment-by-time interaction, ERT status, and gender, as well as the fixed, continuous covariates of baseline 6MWD, baseline age, baseline weight, and baseline height." No baseline×visit term. The 6MWD stratification variable enters as continuous baseline 6MWD.
- Random effects: none (R-matrix only; SAS `repeated AVISIT / type=UN subject=USUBJID`) [SAP App. 3 p.67]
- Covariance: unstructured. Fallback, SAP verbatim: "If this model fails to converge, a compound symmetry (CS) covariance structure will be used instead."
- df: Kenward-Roger ("The Kenward-Roger approximation will be used to estimate denominator degrees of freedom and adjust standard errors for the tests of fixed effects.")
- Estimation: REML
- Time coding: categorical. 4 levels: Weeks 12, 26, 38, 52 [IR p.38]
- LSMEANS: OM (observed margins) and E options. Contrast via `lsmestimate` at Week 52 with one-sided (upper) and two-sided p-values [SAP p.35, p.67]
- Estimand: treatment policy. SAP: "difference ... in mean change in 6MWD from baseline to Week 52, regardless of whether intercurrent events have occurred." FDA [IR p.38]: "the treatment-policy estimand is acceptable and the final acceptability of its estimation based on the MMRM would be a review issue."
- Missing data / intercurrent events: ITT-OBS, no imputation, MAR. Subjects who discontinue drug are withdrawn from the study, so no post-discontinuation data exist apart from the EOS/ET visit, which is mapped into a visit window. SAP Table 5 [p.27-28]: "Data after study discontinuation will be considered missing and will be handled by the MAR assumption in the MMRM analysis." 5 subjects (4 cipa-mig, 1 comparator) were missing Week 52 [IR p.38]. FDA: "the review team found the missing at random assumption reasonable."
- MNAR sensitivity: "control group imputation" [SAP §8.2 p.34]. Each missing Week-52 value is replaced by the mean of 15 draws, with replacement, from observed control-arm Week-52 values, then MMRM is refit. This is a single-imputation control-based approach, not MI with J2R/CR. Results Not stated in IR. Other sensitivity analyses: ANCOVA ITT-LOCF; nonparametric randomization-based ANCOVA if Shapiro-Wilk p<0.01 (triggered: FDA says "The normality assumption required of the MMRM method was violated"); PP ANCOVA; randomization test; ANCOVA with outliers removed (studentized residual >3).
- Software: SAS PROC MIXED, SAS 9.4 (or latest) and R [SAP §8.1 p.33, §8.5.1]
- Result, all ITT [IR Table 19, p.49]: LS-mean change 21.44 (SE 5.75) vs 16.11 (8.58); difference 5.33 m (95% CI −15.21, 25.88), p=0.608 (two-sided). ANCOVA-LOCF 5.91 (−14.17, 26.00), p=0.561. Wilcoxon p=0.116.
- FDA comments: superiority was tested at two-sided 0.05 (equivalent to the SAP's one-sided 0.025). "The primary efficacy results were heavily influenced by the presence of an outlier in the comparator arm." [IR p.43]
- Discrepancy: the README says the "full ITT population" LS-mean difference was 14.21 m with one-sided p=0.048. Per FDA Tables 19/20, 14.21 is the outlier-excluded MMRM (two-sided p=0.0967). The full-ITT MMRM result is 5.33 m, p=0.608. The publication abstract reports LOCF 20.8 vs 7.2 m, difference 13.6 (−2.8 to 29.9).

#### Model 2: 6MWD Week 52, excluding one outlying comparator subject (post hoc sensitivity)

- model_family: MMRM (same specification as Model 1) [IR Table 20 footnote: "MMRM including treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, ERT status, gender, baseline 6MWT, age (continuous), weight, and height; an unstructured covariance matrix was used."]
- Rationale: after database lock, the subject admitted he "deliberately underperformed on the 6MWT and PFT" at screening [IR p.48-49]
- Result [IR Table 20, p.52]: cipa-mig N=85 vs comparator N=37; LS means 21.31 (4.65) vs 7.10 (7.04); difference 14.21 (−2.60, 31.02), p=0.0967. ANCOVA-LOCF 13.96 (−2.72, 30.64), p=0.1002. Wilcoxon p=0.0665.
- FDA: "exclusion of the outlier may be reasonable given the questions of integrity of the subject's efforts"; "although statistical significance is not achieved ... they do provide convincing evidence that cipa-mig provides a clinically meaningful numerical improvement."

#### Model 3: Key secondary endpoints incl. FVC % predicted at Week 52 (supportive MMRM)

- model_family: MMRM
- Role: supportive. The main analysis for key secondaries was ANCOVA on ITT-LOCF [SAP §8.6 p.39]. SAP [p.37]: "each of the other key secondary endpoints will be analyzed using an MMRM analysis on the ITT-OBS population ... similar to what has been described for the primary endpoint analysis."
- Specification: same as Model 1 with the endpoint's baseline value (UN, KR, REML)
- Result: MMRM-specific values Not stated in IR. The FDA-reported FVC result is LS-mean change −1.64 (0.72) vs −3.96 (1.02); difference 2.32% (0.02, 4.62), nominal p=0.0484 [IR Table 15]. FDA's footnote labels this "ANCOVA" but lists "treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction ... an unstructured covariance matrix" with LOCF. The model description is internally inconsistent and it is unclear whether this is a repeated-measures model.
- Formal testing stopped at the primary endpoint (gatekeeping), so FVC is nominal only

#### Model 4: 6MWD — MMRM incorporating handling of intercurrent events (prespecified sensitivity)

- model_family: MMRM
- SAP [Table 7, p.37]: "MMRM analysis incorporating the handling of intercurrent events" (6MWD). FVC uses the ANCOVA counterpart.
- Details beyond the name, and results: Not stated

#### Model 5: Exploratory interaction and subgroup MMRMs (6MWD; FVC subgroups)

- model_family: MMRM
- SAP [p.35-36]: time×covariate (baseline 6MWD, age, weight, ERT status) and treatment×covariate interactions, each added one at a time to the full MMRM; flagged if two-sided p<0.10. MMRM for FVC by baseline FVC <85% vs ≥85% (ITT-OBS) [SAP p.38].
- Results: Not stated (FDA subgroup forest plot used LOCF ANCOVA, not MMRM [IR Fig 13])

Other non-mixed analyses: ANCOVA (PROC MIXED with no REPEATED statement); 12-month rate-of-change, i.e., per-subject OLS slopes compared by ANCOVA (two-stage, not a mixed model); a composite responder analysis with a continuation-logit model; Wilcoxon global test (post hoc, p=0.022).

#### Verbatim specification excerpts

##### Model 1: Change from baseline in 6MWD at Week 52 (primary)

> "The primary efficacy endpoint (change from baseline to Week 52 in 6MWD) will be analyzed using an MMRM model to compare between treatment and control on the ITT-OBS population. For this analysis, the dependent variable is the change from baseline to all post-baseline visits. Independent variables in the model are the fixed, categorical effects of treatment, time (ie, visit), treatment-by-time interaction, ERT status, and gender, as well as the fixed, continuous covariates of baseline 6MWD, baseline age, baseline weight, and baseline height. SAS PROC MIXED will be used for the analysis, with restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML) and unstructured within-subject covariance structure. The Kenward-Roger approximation will be used to estimate denominator degrees of freedom and adjust standard errors for the tests of fixed effects. If this model fails to converge, a compound symmetry (CS) covariance structure will be used instead. The OBSMARGINS (OM) option in the LSMEANS statement will be specified to allow for the use of the observed marginal distributions of the categorical variable rather than assuming a balance among the levels of the categorical variable. The E option will also be specified to check for estimability of LS means."
>
> — SAP Final v3.0 §8.5.1, p. 36 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/62/NCT03729362/SAP_001.pdf)

> "All the relevant estimates from this model, including LS means, standard errors (SE), treatment differences in LS means, and the corresponding 95% CIs will be estimated for each time point. The main variable to be estimated (ie, the estimand) in the primary comparison is the difference between ATB200/AT2221 and alglucosidase alfa/placebo in mean change in 6MWD from baseline to Week 52, regardless of whether intercurrent events have occurred. The significance test will be based on the treatment comparison of LS means at Week 52 and a p-value will be presented for this time point only. Estimated LS means (± SE) for the change from baseline by treatment group will be plotted over time."
>
> — SAP Final v3.0 §8.5.1, p. 37 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/62/NCT03729362/SAP_001.pdf)

> "Data after study discontinuation will be considered missing and will be handled by the MAR assumption in the MMRM analysis."
>
> — SAP Final v3.0 §6.4 Table 5, p. 28 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/62/NCT03729362/SAP_001.pdf)

> "The MMRM analysis will be used as the primary efficacy analysis for the 6MWD regardless of the results of the normality checks, as the MMRM model is believed to be robust against deviations from normality (Bartlett 2014). The nonparametric randomization-based covariance analysis described in Section 8.5.1.2 will be performed as a sensitivity analysis only if the normality assumption is notably violated with the Shapiro-Wilk test p-value < 0.01. The MMRM analysis assumes that data are missing at random (MAR)."
>
> — SAP Final v3.0 §8.2, p. 34 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/62/NCT03729362/SAP_001.pdf)

> "In addition, a ‘control group imputation’ algorithm based on data sampled from the control group (alglucosidase alfa/placebo) will be implemented to replace missing data at the post-baseline visit. For example: For each instance of a missing 6MWD result at Week 52 in either treatment group (ie, active control or new treatment), a random sample of 15 values will be selected (with replacement) from the available set of data in the control group at Week 52. The average of these 15 values will then be used to replace the missing value. These steps will be carried out until all missing data at Week 52 have been replaced. The planned analysis (eg, MMRM) will then be performed on these newly imputed data. Consistency in the results with the original analysis (that is, the treatment effects are in the same direction, and the conclusions are similar) will suggest that the MAR assumption is valid."
>
> — SAP Final v3.0 §8.2, p. 35 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/62/NCT03729362/SAP_001.pdf)

```sas
ods output LSMeans=lsm LSMEstimate=lsmest;
proc mixed data = anadat method = reml;
   class TRTPN AVISIT ERTSTA SEX USUBJID;
   model CHG = TRTPN AVISIT TRTPN*AVISIT SEX BASE ERTSTA AGEBL HGTBL WGTBL /
               ddfm=kr;
   repeated AVISIT / type=UN subject=USUBJID;
   lsmeans TRTPN*AVISIT / slice=AVISIT alpha=0.05 OM diff cl s; *** Obtain
      treatment means and differences at each visit, with CIs.**;

   lsmestimate TRTPN*AVISIT "Treat vs. Control at Week 52" 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 -1
      / upper testvalue=0; *** Get treatment diff and 1-sided p-value **;

   lsmestimate TRTPN*AVISIT ‘Treat vs. Control at Week 52’ 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 -1 /
      testvalue=0 alpha=0.05 cl; **Get treatment diff and 2-sided p-value *;
```

— SAP Final v3.0 Appendix 3 (Sample Code for the MMRM Analysis), p. 68 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/62/NCT03729362/SAP_001.pdf)

> "The statistical analysis plan (SAP; version 3) was finalized on January 14, 2021 and submitted to the Agency on January 19, 2021. The SAP-defined primary estimand for the primary efficacy endpoint is a treatment-policy estimand which is estimated by a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM). The MMRM analysis relies on two assumptions: (1) the primary endpoint has a normal distribution and (2) the missing data are missing at random. The Agency reviewed this SAP and stated that the treatment-policy estimand is acceptable and the final acceptability of its estimation based on the MMRM would be a review issue."

The MMRM included treatment group, time (i.e., study visit), an interaction between time and treatment, ERT experience status, sex, age, baseline 6MWD, weight, and height. Study visit was a categorical variable with four levels (12, 26, 38, and 52 weeks). The unstructured covariance structure was used to account for the within-subject correlations for the repeated measures. The estimate of the effect of the interaction between treatment and time at the 52-week timepoint was used to estimate the treatment effect for the primary endpoint."

### Nedosiran (Rivfloza) — NDA 215842

- Therapeutic area: Rare Disease / Genetic / Metabolic-genetic
- Sponsor: Novo Nordisk, Inc. (c/o Dicerna Pharmaceuticals; Dicerna ran PHYOX2)
- Approval year: 2023 (September 29, 2023)
- Trial: PHYOX2 (DCR-PHXC-201), NCT03847909; 35 randomized (23 nedosiran, 12 placebo)

Context: The primary endpoint (AUC of percent change in 24-h Uox, Days 90-180) used a single-record ANCOVA (treatment, age category, eGFR category, baseline Uox) on 50 FCS multiply-imputed datasets. The SAP fits it with PROC MIXED only so that MIANALYZE gets SEs. There is no RANDOM or REPEATED statement, so it is **not** a mixed model [SAP §6.1.5.1, p.22]. FDA footnotes still label the AUC MI analyses (Tables 85-86 and the rerandomization test) "Calculated using mixed model repeated measures combined using Rubin's rule" [IR §16.2-16.4]. The mixed-model analyses are listed below.

#### Model 1: Rate of change in eGFR (secondary, 6th in fixed-sequence hierarchy)

- Trial/role: PHYOX2. Secondary endpoint, last in the 6-step hierarchy. FDA reported nominal CIs and p-values only.
- model_family: random-coefficients (random intercept + slope)
- Response: observed eGFR (raw)
- Verbatim [SAP §8.3, p.36]: "A linear mixed model with observed eGFR as the dependent variable and treatment, study month and the interaction between treatment and month as independent variable, will be used to estimate rate of decline in eGFR response between DCR-PHXC and placebo treatments. A random intercept and slope will be included in the mixed model to fit a different intercept and slope for each subject. In this analysis nominal month will be modeled as a continuous independent factor."
- Fixed effects: treatment, month (continuous), treatment × month
- Random effects: subject intercept and slope on month (`RANDOM int <Month> / SUB=<participant ID> TYPE=<covariance structure>`)
- Covariance: "To handle the repeated measures data an unstructured variance-covariance matrix will be considered. In the event of convergence issues, a compound symmetric variance-covariance matrix will be used." This applies to the G-matrix TYPE= [SAP §8.3]
- df: Kenward-Roger (`DDFM=KWR`). Estimation: REML (`METHOD=REML`) [SAP code]
- Contrast: difference in slopes via `ESTIMATE "DCR-PHXC versus Placebo" <treatment*Month> 1 -1`. ITT population, one-sided alpha 0.025
- Missing data: likelihood-based on observed data (implicit MAR); no imputation. MNAR sensitivity: Not stated
- Software: SAS 9.4 or higher, PROC MIXED [SAP §4.1]
- Result [IR Table 16, FDA program "fda egfrchange itt.sas", ITT N=12 placebo / 23 nedosiran]: eGFR decline 1.10 vs 0.35 mL/min/1.73 m²/month. Difference -0.75 (95% CI -2.1, 0.6), p=0.14 (nominal).
- FDA comments: FDA's methods text calls it "mixed model repeated measures with a different intercept and slope for each patient" [IR §6]. The result was not significant. FDA said to interpret it "with caution given the baseline imbalances in eGFR … suggesting that patients in the placebo group had more severe/advanced disease at baseline."

#### Model 2: Percent change (and absolute change) in 24-h Uox averaged over Days 90-180 (supportive; FDA reviewer analysis used for labeling)

- model_family: MMRM (compound symmetry)
- Verbatim [IR §6, p.44; repeated in §16.6, p.162]: "…imputing 50 datasets for 24 h urinary oxalate measurements at Days 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, and 180 and then evaluating mean change from baseline of 24 h Uox over Days 90, 120, 150, and 180 for each imputed dataset using mixed model repeated measures with independent factors treatment, eGFR group, age group, baseline 24 h Uox concentration, and visit by treatment interaction, with a compound symmetric covariance matrix, with the results subsequently combined using Rubin's rule."
- Fixed effects: treatment, eGFR group, age group, baseline 24-h Uox, visit × treatment (visit categorical)
- Random effects: none stated. Covariance: CS. Fallback, df, estimation: Not stated
- Estimand: LS-mean percent change averaged over Days 90/120/150/180, nedosiran vs placebo, ITT. Reported for PH1+PH2 and PH1-only
- Missing data: MI (50 imputations, MAR) followed by MMRM and Rubin's rules. FDA ran its own tipping-point delta-shift analysis (nedosiran +0 to +1000 µmol/day; placebo 0 to -1000) on the AUC ANCOVA endpoint, and significance held across all shifts [IR Tables 87-88]
- Software: SAS reviewer programs; version Not stated
- Results, percent change [IR Table 17]:
  - PH1+PH2: placebo 12% (-12, 36), nedosiran -37% (-53, -21); difference -49% (-72, -26), p<0.0001
  - PH1: placebo 6%, nedosiran -50%; difference -56% (-80, -33), p<0.0001
- Results, absolute change [IR Table 18]:
  - PH1+PH2 (N=12/23): 152 vs -514 µmol/day; difference -667 (-1000, -333), p<0.0001
  - PH1 (N=11/18): 83 vs -689; difference -777 (-1125, -418), p<0.0001
  - All results are nominal
- FDA comments: FDA criticized the AUC endpoint as order-dependent ("random highs and lows"). The Applicant's percent-change derivations conflicted with each other. FDA built this analysis and asked that the LS-mean percent change be included in labeling.

#### Model 3: Percent change in 24-h Uox, Days 90-180 — Applicant CSR Table A4 (supportive)

- model_family: MMRM (details sparse)
- Fixed effects [IR §16.6, p.162]: "treatment, baseline urinary oxalate concentration, age group, eGFR group, and study day (90, 120, 150, or 180)"
- Random effects, covariance, df, estimation, software: Not stated
- Result [IR Table 89, PH1 mITT]: placebo 6.5%, nedosiran -52.5%; difference -59% (-81%, -37%), p<0.0001 (nominal)
- FDA comments: these results conflict with the Applicant's AUC/90 estimate (placebo +14.6%), and both conflict with the descriptive trend graph (Fig. 44). FDA replaced them with Model 2.

#### Model 4: Body-weight imputation model for BSA adjustment (data derivation, not efficacy)

- model_family: random-coefficients
- Verbatim [SAP, weight imputation rules]: "missing weight values will be imputed by fitting a mixed model with weight at the dependent variable and study month as the main effect. Random coefficients will be used for the intercept and study month." The SAP code uses `RANDOM INTERCEPT <study month> / SUBJECT=<subject> SOLUTION`. Subject-specific fitted lines (fixed effects plus BLUPs) impute the missing weights.
- Covariance, df: Not stated. Software: SAS PROC MIXED

#### Verbatim specification excerpts

##### Model 1: Rate of change in eGFR (secondary, 6th in fixed-sequence hierarchy)

> "A linear mixed model with observed eGFR as the dependent variable and treatment, study month and the interaction between treatment and month as independent variable, will be used to estimate rate of decline in eGFR response between DCR-PHXC and placebo treatments. A random intercept and slope will be included in the mixed model to fit a different intercept and slope for each subject. In this analysis nominal month will be modeled as a continuous independent factor. The Least Squares adjusted means will be reported for each treatment group as well as the standard errors and 95% confidence intervals for the LS means. The estimate of treatment effect will be reported as the difference in treatment means, 95% confidence interval for the difference in means, the standard error for the mean difference, and the p-value for the treatment difference."
>
> — SAP v1.0 §8.3, p. 37 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/09/NCT03847909/SAP_001.pdf)

```sas
PROC MIXED DATA=<input data> METHOD=REML;
 CLASS <treatment> <participant ID>;
 MODEL <observed eGFR value> = <treatment> <Month> <treatment*Month> / SOLUTION
DDFM=KWR;
RANDOM int <Month> / SUB= <participant ID> TYPE=<covariance structure>;
ESTIMATE "Slope for Treatment='DCR-PHXC " Month 1 <treatment*Month> 1 0 ;
ESTIMATE "Slope for Treatment=Placebo" Month 1 <treatment*Month> 0 1;
ESTIMATE “DCR-PHXC versus Placebo” <treatment*Month> 1 -1 / alpha=0.05 CL;
RUN;
```

— SAP v1.0 §8.3 (example SAS code), p. 37 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/09/NCT03847909/SAP_001.pdf)

> "To handle the repeated measures data an unstructured variance-covariance matrix will be considered. In the event of convergence issues, a compound symmetric variance-covariance matrix will be used."
>
> — SAP v1.0 §8.3, p. 37 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/09/NCT03847909/SAP_001.pdf)

> "These analyses will be performed based on the ITT population. All hypotheses will be tested at the one-sided significance level alpha of 2.5% within the hierarchical testing framework described in section 6.1.4 Multiple Comparisons."
>
> — SAP v1.0 §8.3, p. 37 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/09/NCT03847909/SAP_001.pdf)

> "Percentage normal or near-normal Uox was analyzed using Fisher’s exact test, change from baseline oxalate was analyzed using the exact Wilcoxon two-sample test, and rate of change in eGFR was analyzed using mixed model repeated measures with a different intercept and slope for each patient."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review §6 (Secondary Endpoints), p. 37 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215842Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "Differences between treatment and placebo in rate of eGFR change were not statistically significant (Table 16). Although the point estimates of monthly rate of eGFR decline favor the nedosiran arm, these results should be interpreted with caution given the baseline imbalances in eGFR (median 86 mL/min/1.73 m2 [range 35 to 197 mL/min/1.73 m2] in the nedosiran group and 77 mL/min/1.73 m2 [range 44 to 131 mL/min/1.73 m2] in the placebo group) and differences in 24 h Uox (Table 8) between the treatment arms, suggesting that patients in the placebo group had more severe/advanced disease at baseline."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review §6 (Rate of Change in eGFR), p. 44 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215842Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "Source: Reviewer program fda egfrchange itt.sas, adapted from analysis for CSR Table 21 a Nominal confidence limits and p-value – endpoint selected post hoc without multiplicity adjustment."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review Table 16 source/footnote, p. 43 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215842Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

##### Model 2: Percent change (and absolute change) in 24-h Uox averaged over Days 90-180 (supportive; FDA reviewer analysis used for labeling)

> "The Applicant proposed to include information in Section 14 of the label on the percentage reduction from Baseline in Uox; however, as described in Section 16.6, the Applicant used various methods of calculation which produced conflicting results. To resolve this issue, the review team conducted an ITT analysis for percentage change in Uox directly, imputing 50 datasets for 24 h urinary oxalate measurements at Days 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, and 180 and then evaluating mean change from baseline of 24 h Uox over Days 90, 120, 150, and 180 for each imputed dataset using mixed model repeated measures with independent factors treatment, eGFR group, age group, baseline 24 h Uox concentration, and visit by treatment interaction, with a compound symmetric covariance matrix, with the results subsequently combined using Rubin’s rule."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review §6 (Percentage Reduction in 24 h Urinary Oxalate), p. 45 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215842Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "To address these issues with the approaches used by the Applicant, the review team implemented a single comprehensive intent-to-treat analysis which imputed 50 datasets for 24 h Uox measurements at Days 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, and 180 and then evaluated the mean change from baseline in 24 h urinary oxalate over Days 90, 120, 150, and 180 for each imputed dataset using mixed model repeated measures with independent factors of treatment, eGFR group, age group, Baseline 24 h Uox concentration, and visit by treatment interaction, with a compound symmetric covariance matrix, with the results subsequently combined using Rubin’s rule."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review §16.6, p. 163 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215842Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "Missing data was imputed using the missing-at-random assumption using a fully conditional regression-based multiple imputation model, which included treatment, age category, eGFR category, baseline, and outcomes at Days 90, 120, 150, and 180. For each analysis, 50 imputations were conducted, with the results summarized using Rubin’s method."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review §6 (Missing Data), p. 38 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215842Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

> "Source: Reviewer program primary efficacy urinary oxalate itt all visits lt 2023 04 24.sas. * Statistical significance nominal only – endpoint selected post hoc without multiplicity adjustment. Calculated using mixed model repeated measures combined using Rubin’s rule."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review Table 18 source/footnote, p. 46 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215842Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

##### Model 3: Percent change in 24-h Uox, Days 90-180 — Applicant CSR Table A4 (supportive)

> "The mixed model repeated measures analysis shown in Table A4 in the clinical study report is shown in the last row of Table 89. This analysis included the following independent factors: treatment, baseline urinary oxalate concentration, age group, eGFR group, and study day (90, 120, 150, or 180), but the results conflict with the data used to generate Figure 44 which, in turn, failed to include imputation for missing data and calculated point estimates using simple averages, without any adjustments for covariates."

> "The estimate shown in the first row of Table 89 was obtained by dividing the change from baseline AUC by the number of days over which the AUC was calculated, a method that has not yet been studied in the statistical literature and that has undesirable statistical properties in small studies (see discussion of random highs and lows in Section 16.1 of this review)."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review §16.6, p. 163 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215842Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)

##### Model 4: Body-weight imputation model for BSA adjustment (data derivation, not efficacy)

> "For all participants, regardless of age, missing weight values will be imputed by fitting a mixed model with weight at the dependent variable and study month as the main effect. Random coefficients will be used for the intercept and study month. In this way, the coefficients will vary by subject. The fitted line will be used to impute the missing weight value for a given value of study month."
>
> — SAP v1.0 §6.1.10.3 (Weight Imputations Rules for BSA Adjusted Uox Calculation), p. 32 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/09/NCT03847909/SAP_001.pdf)

```sas
ODS OUTPUT SolutionF = fixed SolutionR = random
PROC MIXED DATA=weightdata;
CLASS <subject>;
MODEL <weight> = <study month> / SOLUTION;
RANDOM INTERCEPT <study month> / SUBJECT = <subject> SOLUTION;
RUN;
```

— SAP v1.0 §6.1.10.3 (example SAS pseudo code), p. 32 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/09/NCT03847909/SAP_001.pdf)

### Vamorolone (Agamree) — NDA 215239

- Therapeutic area: Rare Disease / Genetic / Metabolic-genetic
- Sponsor: Santhera Pharmaceuticals (Switzerland) Ltd. (IND/SAP sponsor ReveraGen BioPharma; Catalyst became applicant later on S-001)
- Approval year: 2023 (October 26, 2023)
- Trial: VBP15-004 (VISION-DMD), NCT03439670; 121 randomized 2:2:1:1:1:1 (vamorolone 2.0 / 6.0 mg/kg, prednisone 0.75 mg/kg, placebo), stratified by age <6 vs ≥6. The SAP covers Period 1 (Weeks 1-24) only.

Common MMRM specification (Models 1-4):

- Verbatim [SAP v3.0 §7.6, p.44]: "…using a restricted maximum likelihood (REML)-based MMRM. This model includes fixed effects for treatment (vamorolone 2.0 mg/kg/day, vamorolone 6.0 mg/kg/day, prednisone 0.75 mg/kg/day, and placebo), age group (<6 years; ≥6 years), week, baseline TTSTAND velocity, and the treatment-by-week interaction. Study week will be included in the model as a categorical variable (Weeks 6, 12, and 24) along with the treatment-by-week interaction." Also: "An unstructured covariance matrix will be used, and underlying modelling assumptions will be checked. If this analysis fails to converge, Akaike's information criterion will be used to select the best covariance structure from compound symmetry and autoregressive-1 (AR(1)). The Kenward-Roger approximation will be used to estimate denominator degrees of freedom."
- FDA [IR §6.2.1.3, p.25-26]: "A restricted maximum likelihood-based mixed model with repeated measures (MMRM) using observed cases without imputations was used… An unstructured covariance structure was applied for the MMRM. The Kenward-Roger method was used to compute the denominator degrees of freedom."
- Random effects: none (R-matrix only). Time: categorical. Estimation: REML
- Population: mITT-1 (randomized, at least 1 dose, at least 1 post-baseline Period-1 assessment)
- Contrasts: LS-mean contrasts at Week 24, all from the single 4-arm model
- Missing data: primary analysis uses observed cases under MAR. Inability to perform a timed test is set to velocity = 0 before analysis
- MNAR sensitivity [SAP §7.3.2.2]: control-based PMM, Copy-Reference (Ratitch & O'Kelly 2011), run in 5 steps:
  1. MCMC MI for intermittent missing data to get a monotone pattern
  2. MAR monotone MI
  3. Reset non-COVID monotone gaps to missing
  4. Copy-Reference MNAR MI (COVID-related missingness stays MAR)
  5. MMRM on each of 1000 imputations, combined with Rubin's rules (PROC MIANALYZE)
- Other sensitivity analyses: MCMC MAR MI (1000 imputations); COVID missing/delayed (>21 days) set to missing; video-assessment data set to missing; TTSTAND floor-truncation at 2.5 s; ITT and complete-data sets
- Software: "SAS (release 9.4 or higher) for Windows" [SAP §7.3.8]

#### Model 1: TTSTAND velocity change at Week 24 (primary: 6.0 mg/kg vs placebo; 1st key secondary: 2.0 mg/kg vs placebo)

- Results [IR Tables 11, 13; FDA reanalysis]:
  - 6.0 mg/kg (N=28): LS mean 0.0483 (SE 0.0136) rises/s; placebo (N=28): -0.0120 (0.0135); difference 0.0603 (0.0230, 0.0976), p=0.0018
  - 2.0 mg/kg (N=30): 0.0328 (0.0131); difference 0.0449 (0.0082, 0.0816), p=0.0171
- Sensitivity [IR Table 12]:
  - MI with copy-reference: 0.0587 (0.0220, 0.0954), p=0.0017
  - Floor truncation: 0.0575 (0.0236, 0.0913), p=0.0011
  - Video assessment set to missing: 0.0606, p=0.0016
  - ITT: 0.0601, p=0.0017
  - Wilcoxon: LOCF p=0.0011; completers p=0.0016
- FDA comments: "Non-parametric Wilcoxon rank sum test was done at Week 24 as a sensitivity analysis because the normality assumption of the primary model was not satisfied." The IR narrative misprints the 2.0 mg/kg LS mean as 0.0483 (Table 13 shows 0.0328). There was no FDA disagreement with the model.

#### Model 2: 6MWT distance change at Week 24 (key secondary; hierarchy steps 2, 3, 6, 7)

- Results:
  - 6.0 mg/kg vs placebo [IR Table 14] (N=28/28): 28.820 (9.392) vs -13.666 (9.884); difference 42.485 m (15.577, 69.394), p=0.0023
  - 2.0 mg/kg vs placebo [IR Table 15]: 26.834 (9.545) vs -13.666; difference 40.50 (13.282, 67.718), p=0.0040
  - The vs-prednisone comparisons were not reached in the hierarchy, and their results were not located in the IR
- FDA comments:
  - The IR narrative contradicts its own tables for both doses: 41.586 m (14.232, 68.940), p=0.0033 and 37.124 m (9.553, 64.696), p=0.0089. The README quotes a mix of the table and narrative values.
  - Baseline 6MWT was shorter in the vamorolone arms.

#### Model 3: TTRW 10-m velocity change at Week 24 (key secondary; steps 4, 5)

- Results:
  - 6.0 mg/kg vs placebo [IR Table 16]: 0.2578 (0.0542) vs 0.0140 (0.0556); difference 0.2439 m/s (0.0932, 0.3945), p=0.0018
  - 2.0 mg/kg vs placebo [IR Table 17]: difference 0.1273 (-0.0263, 0.2809), p=0.1031. The fixed sequence stopped here.

#### Model 4: Other secondary motor endpoints (TTCLIMB velocity, NSAA, knee/elbow myometry, TTSTAND seconds), vs placebo and vs prednisone (secondary, not multiplicity-controlled)

- Uses the same MMRM [SAP §7.6; IR p.26: "same fixed effects, covariate, covariance structure strategy, and method to compute the denominator degrees of freedom"]
- FDA also re-ran these in the PP and completer sets [IR §16]
- Results not extracted

#### Model 5: Multivariate pooled timed-function model (sensitivity for missing 6MWT)

- model_family: other — doubly-repeated (multivariate) MMRM with Kronecker covariance
- Response: percent change from baseline in TTRW velocity, TTCLIMB velocity, and 6MWT, stacked in one model
- Verbatim [SAP §7.6, p.46-47]: "The model will use the Kronecker product covariance structure, as proposed by Galecki (1994). Accordingly, the covariance structure will be set as type=un@ar(1) in the REPEATED statement of the MIXED procedure." SAS code:
  `model chg=age paramcd trtp avisit paramcd*trtp paramcd*avisit trtp*avisit paramcd*trtp*avisit / ddfm=kr; repeated paramcd avisit / subject=usubjid type=un@ar(1);`

- df: Kenward-Roger. Estimation: Not stated (PROC MIXED default REML). The code has no baseline covariate.
- Result: not located in IR
- FDA comments [IR regulatory history, Type C meeting April 29, 2021]: "the sponsor would need to provide justification from literature for using mixed model repeated measures (MMRM) for multiple parameters and should explain how this model is applicable to their case for interpreting 6-minute walk test (6MWT) missing data."

#### Model 6: PD serum biomarkers (adrenal, insulin resistance, bone turnover), Weeks 12 and 24 (secondary PD/safety)

- Specification [SAP §7.9]: REML MMRM with fixed effects treatment, week (categorical), treatment × week, age group, and baseline. UN covariance, with AIC choice of CS or AR(1) if UN fails. Kenward-Roger df. Safety Population, as-treated. HbA1c (one post-baseline value) uses ANCOVA.
- FDA comments [IR safety summary]: an MMRM showed significant BTM differences between vamorolone and prednisone. FDA said "The statistical validity of this retrospective analysis is not clear."

#### Model 7: PARS III subscores (exploratory)

- Specification [SAP §7.8]: REML MMRM with treatment, week, treatment × week, age group, and baseline. Comparisons: each dose vs prednisone and vs placebo. Covariance and df: Not stated. Results: Not stated.

Not mixed models (for completeness): ANCOVA for DXA, TSQM, PODCI, and HbA1c; Fisher's exact test for the TTSTAND responder analysis.

#### Verbatim specification excerpts

##### Model 1: TTSTAND velocity change at Week 24 (primary: 6.0 mg/kg vs placebo; 1st key secondary: 2.0 mg/kg vs placebo)

> "The primary efficacy outcome, TTSTAND (velocity) change from baseline to Week 24, will be compared between the 6.0 mg/kg/day vamorolone group and the placebo group using a restricted maximum likelihood (REML)-based MMRM. This model includes fixed effects for treatment (vamorolone 2.0 mg/kg/day, vamorolone 6.0 mg/kg/day, prednisone 0.75 mg/kg/day, and placebo), age group (<6 years; ≥6 years), week, baseline TTSTAND velocity, and the treatment-by-week interaction. Study week will be included in the model as a categorical variable (Weeks 6, 12, and 24) along with the treatment-by-week interaction. Within this model, pairwise comparisons (using LS mean contrasts) will be made to compare TTSTAND velocity at 24 weeks for vamorolone 6.0 mg/kg/day dose level with placebo (primary efficacy outcome)."
>
> — SAP v3.0 §7.6, p. 44 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/70/NCT03439670/SAP_003.pdf)

> "An unstructured covariance matrix will be used, and underlying modelling assumptions will be checked. If this analysis fails to converge, Akaike’s information criterion will be used to select the best covariance structure from compound symmetry and autoregressive-1 (AR(1)). The Kenward-Roger approximation will be used to estimate denominator degrees of freedom. If differences between baseline characteristics exist between the treatment groups, it will be investigated if adjustment for these characteristics is clinically relevant and necessary. The secondary outcome measures will be compared using similar models."
>
> — SAP v3.0 §7.6, p. 44 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/70/NCT03439670/SAP_003.pdf)

> "The primary analyses for the primary and secondary efficacy variables will be conducted on observed data only; the MMRMs will employ appropriate covariance structures to accommodate missing data as described in Section 7.6."
>
> — SAP v3.0 §7.3.2.2, p. 27 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/70/NCT03439670/SAP_003.pdf)

> "The primary efficacy analysis model (MMRM) makes the assumption that missing data are “missing at random” (MAR). When data are MAR, the missingness of the data does not depend on the missing value after conditioning on the observed data (i.e., prior assessments and baseline covariates). Note that when the missingness of the data depends on the values of the missing variables after conditioning on the observed data, the data are called “missing not at random” (MNAR). In order to assess the MAR assumption, a control-based PMM will be utilized following the method discussed in Ratitch and O’Kelly (2011) for the primary efficacy endpoint. For this study, missing data due to COVID-19 is always assumed to be MAR. For the remaining missing data, assumption of MNAR will be used as shown below, using Copy-Reference imputation."
>
> — SAP v3.0 §7.3.2.2 (Control-based PMM), p. 29 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/70/NCT03439670/SAP_003.pdf)

> "The dataset generated in Step 3 (which contains monotone missing data) will be imputed based on the assumption of MNAR, using Copy-Reference imputation. The MNAR imputation will be based on trajectories in the placebo group, i.e. data from the placebo group only will be used to generate the imputations. For this, the MNAR statement will be used as described below."
>
> — SAP v3.0 §7.3.2.2 Step 4, p. 30 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/70/NCT03439670/SAP_003.pdf)

```sas
proc mi data=imputed2 out=imputed3 nimpute=1 seed=5346434 minimum=0;
class trtp;
by _imputation_;
var age base w6 w12 w24;
monotone regression;
mnar model(w6 w12 w24 / modelobs=(trtp='Placebo'));
run;
```

— SAP v3.0 §7.3.2.2 Step 4, p. 30 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/70/NCT03439670/SAP_003.pdf)

> "After the missing data imputation is completed using the above steps, change from baseline values will be calculated in each of the imputed datasets at each visit. These 1000 datasets will be analyzed using the MMRM described in Section 7.6 for the primary efficacy endpoint. Treatment effects (difference in least squares [LS] means between treatments) from these 1000 analyses will then be combined using Rubin’s Method via the SAS PROC MIANALYZE procedure for each endpoint."
>
> — SAP v3.0 §7.3.2.2 Step 5, p. 31 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/70/NCT03439670/SAP_003.pdf)

> "Data manipulation, tabulation of descriptive statistics, and graphical representations will be performed primarily using SAS (release 9.4 or higher) for Windows."
>
> — SAP v3.0 §7.3.8, p. 37 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/70/NCT03439670/SAP_003.pdf)

> "A restricted maximum likelihood-based mixed model with repeated measures (MMRM) using observed cases without imputations was used for the analysis of primary endpoint (TTSTAND) in the mITT-1 analysis set. The model included TTSTAND velocity values (as changes from baseline) from Week 6, 12, and 24 as dependent values, baseline age (as stratified at randomization), group (vamorolone 2.0 mg/kg, vamorolone 6.0 mg/kg, prednisone 0.75 mg/kg, or placebo), week (Week 6, 12, or 24), and treatment-by-week interaction as fixed effect, and baseline TTSTAND velocity as a covariate. Within this model, pairwise comparisons (using LSM contrasts) of TTSTAND velocity at Week 24 were made for vamorolone 6.0 mg/kg with [...] placebo. An unstructured covariance structure was applied for the MMRM. The Kenward-Roger method was used to compute the denominator degrees of freedom."

> "Multiple Imputation (MI): After imputation of all intermittent missing data with MI assuming MAR to generate a dataset with monotone missing data structure, all monotone missing data were imputed with MI assuming MAR to general dataset with no missing data. All visits that have monotone missing data that are not due to COVID-19 were set back as missing. Then, remaining monotone missing data which was not related to COVID-19 were imputed with MI assuming MNAR (Copy-reference imputation). The same MMRM was conducted with imputed data and combine results from the analyses."

##### Model 5: Multivariate pooled timed-function model (sensitivity for missing 6MWT)

> "First, the test data will be standardized by using the percentage change from baseline as the endpoint. The percentage change will be calculated as (value at visit – baseline value) / baseline value x 100%, calculated from the endpoints as used in the original statistical analysis, i.e. from velocities or distances. All the percentual change values from the three tests, TTRW, TTCLIMB, and 6MWT, will be entered to a single statistical model."
>
> — SAP v3.0 §7.6, p. 46 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/70/NCT03439670/SAP_003.pdf)

> "A model similar to the MMRM model presented in this SAP will be used, but in addition to the fixed factors included in the MMRM detailed above, the parameter (TTRW velocity, TTCLIMB velocity, or 6MWT) and all 2- and 3-level interaction terms between treatment group, visit and parameter will be added. The model will use the Kronecker product covariance structure, as proposed by Galecki (1994). Accordingly, the covariance structure will be set as type=un@ar(1) in the REPEATED statement of the MIXED procedure. The SAS code for implementing this kind of model with the MIXED procedure is provided by Gao et al. (2006) and outlined below."
>
> — SAP v3.0 §7.6, p. 46 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/70/NCT03439670/SAP_003.pdf)

```sas
proc mixed;
class usubjid age paramcd trtp avisit;
model chg=age paramcd trtp avisit paramcd*trtp paramcd*avisit trtp*avisit
      paramcd*trtp*avisit / ddfm=kr;
repeated paramcd avisit / subject=usubjid type=un@ar(1);
run;
```

— SAP v3.0 §7.6, p. 47 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/70/NCT03439670/SAP_003.pdf)

> "The statistical review team noted that the sponsor would need to provide justification from literature for using mixed model repeated measures (MMRM) for multiple parameters and should explain how this model is applicable to their case for interpreting 6-minute walk test (6MWT) missing data in Study VBP15-004."
>
> — FDA Integrated Review regulatory history (Type C meeting, April 29, 2021), p. 118 (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2023/215239Orig1s000IntegratedR.pdf)
